articles.title: This unique retro dock adds a flip-up display, Thunderbolt 5, & 8TB storage to your Mac [Video]
articles.summary: Amid all the craziness of this iPhone launch week, one of my favorite brands has released its brand-new retro-style dock for the Mac mini and the Mac Studio. Last year, they released their Retro Dock for the M4 Mac mini, and it was the perfect combination of functionality, form, and nostalgia that I had never seen before. It added a ton of ports, an NVMe storage slot, a 5-inch display, all wrapped up in a housing that looked like the original Macintosh from 1984. The new Wokyis G5 & G7 takes it to a whole other level. They’ve added even more pro-level ports, a larger display, usable tactile buttons, while still keeping that retro style look and feel, and they’ve expanded it to both the Mac mini and the Mac Studio. Here is what you need to know. more…

articles.title: 6 reasons I still haven’t bought a Google TV projector (and why I may never get one)
articles.summary: Credit: Rita El Khoury / Android Authority The cheap projector market really took off a few years ago, and the market was suddenly flooded with units ranging from $50 to well over $500. During that time, I invested in a cheap but decent little unit for around $100 that had HDMI support and came with a Roku in the box. While certainly not capable of replacing a TV at this level, it was a great way to watch movies outdoors and gave me a taste of what projector life might be. I reasoned that if these cheap units were this capable, then a real higher-priced projector could likely take me much further. Recently, our living room TV has started showing signs that its days are numbered, and I’ve once again started researching the best projectors . I have to admit I strongly considered a Google TV

articles.title: Kvaesitso is unlike any Android launcher I’ve used — and you won’t find it on the Play Store
articles.summary: Credit: Pankil Shah / Android Authority For years, the best Android launcher wasn’t much of a debate — Nova Launcher had it locked down. But ever since its acquisition, that’s changed, and a lot of us have been left launcher-hopping. I’d been in that same boat, and while Niagara and Lawnchair both came close, neither one made me want to stop looking. And the reason it took me this long to find the perfect launcher is that I kept looking in the one place the answer wasn’t — the Play Store. Kvaesitso is a free, open-source launcher that skips Google’s app store entirely, and it’s unlike anything you’ve probably tried before.

articles.title: Google is hiding a helpful Camera Looks shortcut on the Pixel 11 — how to enable it
articles.summary: The Google Pixel 11 may not look dramatically different from the past couple of generations, but there are some meaningful upgrades across the board. As always, the company has made improvements to the camera hardware. The base Pixel 11 gets an upgraded main camera sensor that captures 56% more light, while the Pro models feature a new 48MP telephoto camera that lets in 30% more light. Of course, those aren’t the only camera upgrades this year. articles.title: Chip Huyen explains how to cut inference costs without new hardware
articles.summary: Last October, the P99 conference — the online gathering for developers focused on high-performance, low-latency applications — featured a cracking keynote from Chip Huyen.  The author of the best-selling AI Engineering , Huyen opened with simple math: Training a frontier model is a one-off cost, but inference is the same cost paid over and over. That’s great for the frontier model providers, and bad for us token burners. Over the life of a model, Huyen reckons the compute split ratio lands somewhere between 1:10 and 1:100 for training to inference. Reasoning models — which burn even more tokens — push that out even further. We all know the feeling of hitting our weekly session quotas. Huyen’s point is that if inference is too expensive, then nobody

articles.title: It passed CI. It passed your evals. The customer still got the wrong answer.
articles.summary: A diff is not evidence. It’s a statement of intent. The tests passed. The review’s done. The change is live. Then someone says the app is slow, or the answers are wrong, or both. You open the diff. Your assistant points at the function it changed and offers a plausible cause. It sounds right. It might not be. This is the observability gap that AI features expose. Dynatrace’s 2026 State of SRE and Platform Engineering report (919 enterprise leaders surveyed globally) found that while 77% of platform engineering teams embed observability in at least some services, only 40% have it fully integrated across all deployments. That gap was manageable when your services were deterministic. But with AI agents, it becomes a liability. A conventional service fails loudly… An A

articles.summary: The AI industry is confronting a growing tension between racing to build more powerful systems and concerns that those systems could become harder to understand and control. (Source: Bloomberg)

articles.title: UK Tech Spinouts Are Struggling Outside the Golden Triangle
articles.summary: Much of the world’s wastewater is still treated using a century-old, energy-intensive process of pumping oxygen through tanks of sewage. Thames Water, the UK’s largest water company, is now trialing an alternative developed at Newcastle University that uses microbes and electrodes to break down waste. It both uses less energy and gives off ammonia that can be recovered and sold as fertilizer.

I’m poking at a laptop at John Deere’s corporate office in Santa Clara, California. There’s a cable connecting the computer to a 5130ML tractor sitting on the grass nearby. A bright red notification sits on the screen, telling me something is wrong.
